title: Sliding Window Beats Linear Attention
hook: The cheap baseline nobody bothered to run wins: sliding-window attention with sinks matches or beats retrofitted linear-attention models, and needs no post-training at all.
key_points: Compares sliding window attention (SWA) with attention sinks against LLMs post-trained to use linear attention.
SWA performs as well or better across multiple LLMs and downstream tasks.
On long-context retrieval (Needle-in-a-Haystack, BABILong) SWA scores 2-10x higher than linear attention.
SWA needs zero post-training — you just change how inference reads the cache.
Authors conclude linear attention likely needs training from scratch, or heavy post-training, to even match SWA.
content_html: Full attention is quadratic: every token you generate adds keys and values that must be kept in memory indefinitely. Linear attention promises to fix this by replacing the growing cache with a fixed-size recurrent state, and a lot of recent work has gone into post-training existing LLMs to use it. Jolicoeur-Martineau and colleagues point out that this line of research has never been carefully compared to the simplest alternative — and when you do compare, the simple thing wins.
extra_html:
The result

Sliding window attention with attention sinks — keep only the last N tokens plus a few special anchor tokens — performs as well or better than post-trained linear attention across several LLMs and downstream tasks. On long-context reasoning benchmarks (Needle-in-a-Haystack, BABILong) the gap is dramatic: the authors report SWA scoring two to ten times higher. This is the regime where a fixed-size state has to throw away exactly the detail the task asks for.

Why it matters

SWA is not a new method; it is the baseline. The paper's contribution is showing that the baseline was skipped, and that the practical recommendation for cutting inference memory should therefore be "switch to SWA" rather than "post-train a linear model." The authors do not claim linear attention is worthless — their read is that it may need to be trained from scratch, or post-trained far more heavily, before it earns its complexity. It is a good example of how a missing baseline can distort a whole research direction.

related.title: Attention Is All You Need
related.hook: Drop recurrence and convolution, keep only attention — and you get a model that trains in parallel and powers nearly every LLM since.

related.title: KV Cache Eviction, Formalized
related.hook: Everyone drops KV cache entries with clever heuristics. Formalize the problem properly and it turns into expectation estimation — which finally lets you correct for what you threw away.

flashcards.prompt: What problem do both sliding-window and linear attention try to solve?
flashcards.back_html: The quadratic cost of full attention: every new token's keys and values must be stored forever, so memory and energy grow without bound as context lengthens.

flashcards.prompt: On long-context retrieval tasks, how did SWA compare to post-trained linear attention?
flashcards.explanation_html: The paper reports a large SWA advantage on Needle-in-a-Haystack and BABILong, which is where a compressed fixed-size recurrent state hurts most.

flashcards.prompt: Why is 'requires no post-training' the paper's strongest practical claim?
flashcards.back_html: Retrofitting linear attention costs a training run per model. SWA is an inference-time change to which keys and values you keep, so the memory saving is available immediately and for free.
